name: franklin
style: Adult male documentary narrator, warm and grounded, American English. Curious and quick on the opening question, clear and steady through the journey; place names, dates and numbers a beat slower. When the second message is written around the edges of the old note, slow down and soften, almost quiet. Say "Erebus" as ERR-uh-bus and "Inuit" as IN-oo-it; "Inuk" as IN-ook. No hype, no shouting. The last line lands with quiet weight.

lines.text: In 1845, two British ships sailed into the Arctic with food for three years.
Why did it take 169 years to find them?
The answer is on this route, and in a note no one found for eleven years.
Sir John Franklin had 129 men, steam engines, and orders to finish the Northwest Passage.
In the summer of 1845, whalers saw the ships in Baffin Bay.
No European saw them again.
They spent their first winter in the harbour of Beechey Island.
Three men died there.
Searchers later found their graves, but no note saying where the ships went.
In 1846 they sailed south, and took the west side of King William Island.
It was the wrong side.
The ice there doesn't always melt in summer.
In September, the ice closed around both ships, and held them for nineteen months.
In May 1847, officers left a note on the shore.
It said: "All well."
They were less than 150 kilometres from waters already on the map.
A year later, someone wrote around the edges of that same note.
Twenty-four men were dead, Franklin among them.
The other 105 had left the ships, and would walk south.
Then the note went back under the stones.
And here is the twist.
In 1854, Inuit told John Rae what they knew: men dragging a boat south, starving.
In London, the story was attacked.
Charles Dickens himself wrote against it.
One search ship, Resolute, was abandoned in the ice.
Its timber became the desk in the Oval Office.
The note was found in 1859, under those stones.
But the ships stayed lost.
In 2014, Erebus was found in waters where Inuit stories had long said a big ship sank.
Two years later, an Inuk hunter remembered a mast in the ice.
Terror lay in that bay.
Food for three years.
A hundred and sixty-nine years to find them.
The Inuit had been telling the story since 1854.
